best-broadway-shows-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of theater interrupted. That season, cut dramatically short by the pandemic shutdown, produced a small but notable collection of productions that ranged from bold reimaginings of classics to powerful new voices finally reaching the Broadway stage.

Leading our rankings is a grittier reboot of **Les Misérables** at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre, earning an 82/100 from critics who largely embrace its fresh approach, though the production hasn't won over everyone. Close behind, **A Soldier's Play** stands as one of the season's most significant achievements—Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama made its long-overdue Broadway debut in a stellar revival that critics found powerfully relevant, scoring 78/100 across 29 reviews.

The remaining productions showcase the season's diversity: Laura Linney's solo turn in **My Name is Lucy Barton** divides critics between admiration for her luminous performance and questions about the adaptation itself, while **Grand Horizons** offers familiar but well-executed boulevard comedy elevated by Jane Alexander's performance. Rounding out our list, Ivo van Hove's radical **West Side Story** reimagining proves the most polarizing, with critics split between those praising its bold vision and those finding it misguided.

With an average score of 74/100 across these five productions, the 2020 season—brief though it was—delivered thoughtful revivals and important theatrical moments that continue to resonate. Whether you're catching final performances or exploring what these shows represent in Broadway's evolution, each offers a distinct theatrical experience worth considering.

best-broadway-shows-2021.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows from 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2021 represent a remarkable chapter in theater history—a season of reopening after unprecedented closure, marked by both bold experimentation and triumphant returns.

The class of 2021 demonstrates exceptional range, from intimate docudramas to lavish spectacles. Leading the pack is "Dana H.," Lucas Hnath's unconventional piece featuring Deirdre O'Connell's mesmerizing lip-sync performance to a real interview with his mother. Critics consistently describe it as unforgettable, even as it challenges traditional theatrical conventions. Rebecca Frecknall's immersive "Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club" follows closely, transforming the August Wilson Theatre into a complete environmental experience that critics hail as definitive. Meanwhile, "The Phantom of the Opera" proves that Andrew Lloyd Webber's mega-musical retains its spectacular power, even as it approached its historic final curtain.

The season also showcases powerful solo performances in "Lackawanna Blues," where Ruben Santiago-Hudson embodies dozens of characters, and verbatim theater in "Is This A Room," which transforms an FBI transcript into gripping drama. Revivals shine particularly bright, with Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped "Company" offering fresh perspective on Sondheim's masterwork, while newer works like Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's "Pass Over" and Lynn Nottage's "Clyde's" bring urgent contemporary voices to Broadway stages.

With an average critic score of 81/100 across these ten productions, the 2021 season proves that Broadway's reopening brought not just a return to normalcy, but a surge of artistic ambition and achievement. Whether you're drawn to experimental forms or classic spectacle, these shows offer compelling reasons to experience what made this season unforgettable.

best-broadway-plays-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway plays that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of theatrical ambition cut short by unprecedented circumstances. Despite the season's abrupt end, these five productions showcase the range and vitality that defined Broadway before the pandemic shutdown.

Leading our rankings is **Les Misérables** (82/100), a grittier reboot of the beloved musical that reimagines the classic at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre. Critics largely embrace this darker interpretation, though purists remain divided on the departure from tradition. Close behind is **A Soldier's Play** (78/100), Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama that finally receives its long-overdue Broadway debut. This stellar revival demonstrates how the play's examination of race, power, and identity within the military remains urgently relevant decades after it was written.

The season also features notable experiments in theatrical form. **My Name is Lucy Barton** (71/100) presents Laura Linney in a solo adaptation of Elizabeth Strout's novel, with critics praising Linney's luminous performance even as they debate the effectiveness of the adaptation itself. Meanwhile, **West Side Story** (68/100) arrives in Ivo van Hove's radical reimagining, incorporating video design and contemporary staging that polarizes audiences and critics alike.

With an average score of 74/100 across these five productions, the 2020 Broadway season demonstrates both artistic ambition and the enduring appeal of powerful storytelling. Whether you're discovering these shows for the first time or revisiting old favorites, our detailed reviews will help you navigate what remains a compelling, if abbreviated, theatrical season.

best-broadway-plays-2021.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the 2021 Broadway season stands as a remarkable period of theatrical renewal and innovation. Following an unprecedented 18-month shutdown, the industry returned with a diverse slate of productions that ranged from intimate docudramas to lavish revivals, earning an impressive average critic score of 81/100.

The season's most acclaimed production is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama featuring Deirdre O'Connell's stunning lip-sync performance. Critics consistently describe the work as mesmerizing and unforgettable, cementing its place as one of the decade's most daring theatrical experiments. Close behind is **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club**, Rebecca Frecknall's immersive reimagining that transforms the August Wilson Theatre into a decadent nightclub, earning widespread acclaim for both its staging innovation and artistic vision.

The season demonstrates remarkable range, from the epic scope of **The Lehman Trilogy** to the verbatim precision of **Is This a Room**, from Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company** to the pop exuberance of **SIX**. Even **The Phantom of the Opera**, entering its final years, receives renewed critical appreciation for its enduring theatrical magic. Meanwhile, solo performances in **Lackawanna Blues** and intimate dramas like **Pass Over** and **Clyde's** showcase the season's commitment to diverse storytelling voices.

These ten productions represent a cross-section of Broadway's triumphant return—a mix of bold experimentation, thoughtful revivals, and populist entertainment that collectively redefined what theater could be in a post-pandemic world. Whether you're drawn to avant-garde innovation or classic spectacle, this guide highlights the productions that critics and audiences continue to celebrate five years later.

best-broadway-plays-2022.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays from 2022

As we look back from March 2026, the 2022 Broadway season stands as a remarkable period of theatrical achievement, marked by an extraordinary concentration of Pulitzer Prize-winning works and critically acclaimed revivals that have left a lasting impact on American theater.

Leading the pack is **Kimberly Akimbo**, the quirky musical about a teenager with a rare aging condition that critics consistently praise as a near-perfect blend of comedy and heartbreak. The show's ability to find humor and humanity in unusual circumstances exemplifies the season's willingness to embrace unconventional storytelling.

The year also proved to be a celebration of theatrical giants, both past and present. **Into the Woods** offered audiences a stripped-down revival that served as a poignant tribute to Stephen Sondheim, while **A Strange Loop** showcased Michael R. Jackson's brazenly original voice in a meta-musical that pushed boundaries and challenged conventions. Tom Stoppard's **Leopoldstadt**, meanwhile, delivered a deeply personal meditation on Jewish identity and the Holocaust that resonated with profound emotional weight.

Perhaps most striking is the prevalence of Pulitzer Prize winners in this lineup—five productions feature Pulitzer-winning plays, including Suzan-Lori Parks' **Topdog/Underdog**, Stephen Adly Guirgis's **Between Riverside and Crazy**, Paula Vogel's **How I Learned to Drive**, and Martyna Majok's **Cost of Living**. This concentration of award-winning work underscores 2022's significance as a season that brought essential American voices to Broadway stages.

With an impressive average critic score of 83/100 across these ten productions, the 2022 season offers theatergoers a diverse array of compelling options, from intimate solo shows to sweeping ensemble pieces.

best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2023

As of March 2026, the Broadway plays that opened in 2023 continue to demonstrate exceptional staying power, with several productions still captivating audiences more than two years after their debuts. This collection of ten productions maintains an impressive average critic score of 82/100, reflecting a particularly strong season for dramatic theater.

Leading the field is Maria Friedman's acclaimed revival of **Merrily We Roll Along**, which has triumphantly redeemed Stephen Sondheim's notorious 1981 flop through emotionally resonant performances and thoughtful direction. The production shares top honors with **Stranger Things: The First Shadow**, a West End transfer that has defied expectations by transcending its franchise origins to deliver technically stunning, jaw-dropping theatrical spectacle.

Other standout productions include Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's **Appropriate**, featuring a blistering ensemble led by Sarah Paulson in this searing family drama that critics have embraced as a modern masterpiece. The timely revival of **Parade**, starring Ben Platt and Micaela Diamond, continues to resonate with its urgent relevance, while the long-overdue return of Ossie Davis's **Purlie Victorious** proves that sharp satire remains bracingly relevant across generations.

The season also showcases remarkable range, from Alex Edelman's brilliant solo show **Just for Us** to the immersive rock studio drama **Stereophonic**, which critics have hailed as a near-perfect theatrical experience despite its demanding three-hour runtime. James Ijames's Pulitzer-winning **Fat Ham** brings raucous humor to its Hamlet-inspired story set at a Black family barbecue, rounding out a season that demonstrates Broadway's continued commitment to bold, diverse voices.

Whether you're seeking musical revivals, intimate solo performances, or expansive ensemble dramas, these productions represent the best of what Broadway theater offered in 2023.

best-broadway-plays-2024.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2024

As of March 2026, the Broadway shows that debuted in 2024 continue to demonstrate remarkable staying power and critical acclaim. This collection of ten productions—averaging an impressive 83/100 critic score—represents one of the strongest theatrical years in recent memory, spanning intimate character studies, historical epics, and bold experimental works.

Leading the field is **Stereophonic**, David Adjmi's meticulously crafted drama about a 1970s rock band in the studio. With a score of 89/100 across 22 reviews, critics consistently describe it as a theatrical marvel that captures the messy, exhilarating reality of the creative process. Close behind is **Operation Mincemeat**, the grassroots British sensation that earned its Broadway transfer through sheer inventive energy and ensemble brilliance.

The year's offerings reveal Broadway's expanding artistic range. **Maybe Happy Ending** brings an unexpectedly touching robot love story to musical theater, while Cole Escola's **Oh, Mary!** reimagines Mary Todd Lincoln as a cabaret-obsessed narcissist in what critics call a comedic tour de force. Traditional revivals also shine, with Audra McDonald bringing fresh depth to Mama Rose in **Gypsy** and a lavish new **Oliver!** balancing spectacle with Dickensian grit.

More intimate works like **Mary Jane**, Amy Herzog's understated drama about maternal devotion in crisis, prove equally powerful alongside ambitious dance-theater hybrids like **Illinoise** and educational musicals like **Suffs**.

Whether you're drawn to rock-and-roll authenticity, absurdist comedy, or emotionally resonant revivals, the class of 2024 offers exceptional options still playing nearly two years after their debuts.

best-broadway-plays-2025.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2025

As March 2026 arrives, the Broadway plays that opened throughout 2025 continue to demonstrate remarkable range and vitality. This season's offerings span from bold reimaginings of American classics to innovative new works tackling contemporary themes, with an impressive average critic score of 85 out of 100 across the ten productions featured here.

Ivo van Hove's stripped-down revival of **All My Sons** leads the field, earning widespread critical acclaim for its emotional intensity and minimalist approach to Arthur Miller's family tragedy. The production's exceptional ensemble work proves that classic American drama remains as powerful as ever when given fresh interpretive vision.

The season also celebrates theatrical nostalgia done right, with the 20th-anniversary revival of **The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee** charming critics with its combination of sharp writing and emotional depth. Meanwhile, **Paddington The Musical** showcases technical theatrical innovation, with reviewers marveling at the remarkably lifelike bear puppet that brings the beloved character to stage life.

Contemporary voices make their mark as well, particularly Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer Prize-winning **English**, which earns strong praise for its nuanced exploration of language and identity. Musical theater fans find much to celebrate in David Yazbek's darkly comic **Dead Outlaw** and a timely revival of **Ragtime** featuring Joshua Henry's powerhouse performance.

From Mel Brooks' irreverent comedy in **The Producers** to Bryna Turner's ambitious **Liberation**, this collection represents Broadway's continued commitment to both preserving theatrical heritage and pushing creative boundaries. Use this guide to discover which productions align with your theatrical interests.

best-broadway-plays-2026.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2026

March 2026 brings a notably lean opening schedule for new Broadway plays, with just one production making its debut this month. While the limited roster reflects the challenging economics facing straight plays on Broadway, the sole entry demonstrates the enduring appeal of well-crafted psychological drama.

**Bug** stands as the month's singular offering, marking the long-awaited Broadway premiere of Tracy Letts' 1996 psychological thriller. With a solid critic score of 74/100 across 35 reviews, the production earns mostly positive notices for its intense exploration of paranoia and delusion. Originally produced by Chicago's Red Orchid Theatre three decades ago, the play arrives on Broadway with renewed relevance, its themes of conspiracy and fractured reality resonating in contemporary discourse. Critics particularly praise the production's claustrophobic staging and committed performances, though some note the material's deliberately unsettling nature may not appeal to all theatergoers.

The sparse March schedule underscores a broader trend in commercial theater, where plays increasingly struggle to secure Broadway berths amid rising production costs and risk-averse producers. That **Bug** makes it to the Great White Way at all speaks to both the strength of Letts' reputation—bolstered by his Pulitzer Prize-winning **August: Osage County**—and the theater community's ongoing commitment to provocative, challenging work.

For audiences seeking substantive dramatic fare this month, **Bug** offers a compelling if confronting option that showcases the raw power of theatrical storytelling. Those planning their spring theater calendar should consider catching this production while monitoring announcements for upcoming play openings in the months ahead.
